title: Spring Boot DevTools

richText: adds development features to an existing Spring Boot application. It is an optional module.
Its restart feature reloads application classes after compiled files change.
Its LiveReload feature asks a connected browser to refresh after resources change.
Spring Boot also applies development settings, such as disabling template caching.
DevTools watches directories on the application classpath.
An edited Java source file must be compiled before DevTools detects the change.
A restart closes the application context and creates a new one. It recreates application beans.
DevTools uses a separate classloader for application classes. It does not edit a running method in place.
Static resources and templates normally trigger LiveReload without restarting the application.

example.title: Restart a Maven application with DevTools
description: Java `17` and Maven are required. The files form a separate project rooted at `pom.xml`.
The application starts through the IDE or the command below.
explanation: `optional` prevents another Maven project from receiving DevTools through this project.
After editing an application class, the IDE build or `mvn compile` updates its compiled class.
DevTools detects that class change and restarts the application.
A compatible LiveReload browser extension must connect to the DevTools server before browser refresh works.

richText: A JVM system property with the same setting, applied before startup, also prevents the restart classloader from being initialized.
Temporarily disabling restart can help identify a classloader conflict.
Spring Boot repackaging excludes DevTools by default. A packaged application launched with
DevTools is for development. Forcing it on in a production process exposes development features.

summary: DevTools restarts an application after compiled code changes and can refresh a connected browser.
